solution:
True.

The chapter lists terrorism as the first and biggest challenge to human security. It explains why: terrorism targets common, innocent people and aims at creating terror or fear in their minds, so that they begin to feel insecure. Human security means human-centric thinking, in which human beings should be protected from all sorts of dangers and should get the opportunities of education, health and development. People who live in fear cannot be said to be protected in this way, and they cannot use such opportunities either.

The chapter therefore concludes in its own words, 'in order to protect human security, it is necessary to put an end to terrorism.' Terrorism is also called the biggest challenge to India's internal security, and the chapter says it is a global problem and that India is making efforts to end it.

True.

The chapter opens by saying that the primary national interest of a country includes defence from foreign aggression and internal unrest and keeping the borders safe, and that 'for this, every nation creates a defence system at the national level.' India has also created such a system.

The reason is that the international system is made up of sovereign nations, and even though they cooperate with each other, conflicts arise between them over boundaries, over water sharing, over the non-observance of international treaties, over constant competition, and over the influx of refugees. Such conflicts are first sought to be resolved by compromise and discussion, but when that is not enough a nation may even think of war. When one nation attacks another and challenges its sovereignty, the security of that nation is endangered.

Because such a danger can arise at any time, the chapter says a nation's first duty and responsibility is to keep its security systems always well-prepared and ready, and that this is what is called National Security. A nation also has to increase its military might and use modern technology to predict threats, build weapon systems and modernise its defence forces.

[Note: the chapter says every nation creates a defence system and must keep it well-prepared and ready; it does not use the word 'strong' about every nation's system, and it separately points out that all countries are not at par with respect to military might.]

False.

The chapter states the opposite in plain words: 'There are several disputes between India and Pakistan.' It then names them as examples — the Kashmir issue, disputes over river water sharing, the problem of infiltrations and the dispute over the border.

The chapter also says that right from the time of independence, Pakistan and China have tried to threaten India's National Security. India, for its part, has continually tried to solve these issues through discussion and negotiations, which itself shows that the issues exist and have not disappeared. So it is wrong to say that there are no issues of dispute between India and Pakistan.

The Rapid Action Force is one of India's paramilitary forces. Paramilitary forces are neither completely military forces nor completely civil forces, and their main task is to help the defence forces.

The special function of the Rapid Action Force is to bring people's lives back to normalcy by moving in quickly in incidents of threat to National Security, such as bomb blasts or riots. Because it acts fast, it is useful exactly where a situation has suddenly gone out of control and order has to be restored at once.

Along with the other paramilitary forces it also shares the responsibility for the security of important locations like railway stations, oil depots and water reserves, and it plays a role in the management of disasters, whether natural or man-made.

In the post-Cold war period the concept of national security changed and became broader. It came to be understood that national security is not just the security of the country but also of the people living in it, because security is ultimately for the people. Human security therefore refers to human-centric thinking.

In human security it is expected that human beings should be protected from all sorts of dangers and that they should be given the opportunities of education, health and development. The concept also includes the idea that a conducive environment should be created for everybody to live a respectable life by overcoming illiteracy, poverty, superstition and backwardness. Human security further necessitates the protection of the rights of minorities and weaker sections.

The chapter names two big challenges to human security — terrorism, which targets common, innocent people and creates fear in their minds, and pollution and other changes in the environment, together with diseases like AIDS, chikungunia, swine flu, ebola and corona. Protecting human beings from such diseases is also considered a factor of human security.

The Home Guards is an organisation that was established in the pre-independence period. Through it, ordinary citizens can join and assist in the defence of the country. Any citizen, man or woman, between the ages of 20 to 35 years can join the Home Guards.

The force has the following tasks: to maintain public security; to keep up the supply of milk, water and other essential services during riots or strikes; to regulate traffic; and to help people at the time of natural disasters like floods and earthquakes.

In this way the Home Guards allows common people themselves to take part in the security of the country and to be useful in times of trouble.

Threats to national security come both from outside the country and from within it.

From outside, conflicts arise between sovereign nations over boundaries, over water sharing, over the non-observance of the terms of international treaties, over constant competition with one another, and over the influx of refugees from neighbouring countries. When such conflicts cannot be settled by compromise and discussion, a nation may even think of war, and when one nation attacks another and challenges its sovereignty, the security of that nation is endangered. Such challenges are created by the military power of aggressive nations, and arms races increase the sense of insecurity further.

In India's own case, right from the time of independence Pakistan and China have tried to threaten India's National Security. With Pakistan there are several disputes — the Kashmir issue, disputes over river water sharing, the problem of infiltrations and the dispute over the border. With China, India had to go to war in 1962; China is trying to establish its hegemony over India's neighbours, which creates tension in Sino-Indian relations, and there is also a border dispute between the two countries.

India's security is threatened from within as well. Religion, regionalism, several rebellious movements based on ideology, race-ethnicity and economic inequality are creating instability, and the Naxalite movement is given as an example of a threat to India's internal security. Terrorism is the biggest challenge to India's internal security; it is a global problem and India is making efforts to end it.

The Border Security Force is one of India's paramilitary forces, whose main task is to help the defence forces.

Its own functions are to create a sense of security in the minds of the people living in areas near the border, to prevent smuggling, and to patrol the border.

As a paramilitary force it also shares the general responsibilities of that group. The responsibility of protecting the country's international borders during peace time rests with the paramilitary forces. They are responsible for the security of important locations like railway stations, oil depots and water reserves, and they play a role in the management of disasters, whether natural or man-made.

| Name of the Security Force | Functions | Chief | Name of the Present Chief |
|---|---|---|---|
| Army | Protecting the geographical boundaries of the country | General | Changes over time — refer to a current source |
| Navy | Protecting the coastline | Admiral | Changes over time — refer to a current source |
| Air Force | Protection of India's air space | Air Chief Marshall | Changes over time — refer to a current source |

The Army, the Navy and the Air Force are the three forces that defend the country, and all three are controlled by the Ministry of Defence. The Indian Army is very big — it is the world's seventh largest. To maintain coordination between the three defence forces, the post of 'Chief of Defence Staff' was created in 2019. All these chiefs are appointed by the President, who is the supreme commander of the defence forces.

[Note: the last column asks for the name of the present chief of each force. The chapter gives only the title of each chief — General, Admiral and Air Chief Marshall — and never names any officer holding these posts. These appointments also change from time to time, so the correct name must be looked up in a current source at the time of answering rather than taken from the textbook.]
